text: Delinquents, scum, people: three columns on a classroom wall, with every pupil's name card hung under one of them. Kobayashi, who built the chart, means it as a ladder. It is 1980 in a small Japanese town, and Sadatomo, barely noticed at home, moves down it when he and his friends lift a few things from a shop for the fun of it. Their fathers are told. The punishment is thirty pages of self-criticism, and the essay he hands in, called I am an onion, strikes his teacher as the first evidence of a soul. Furumaya spends the rest of the film on what that exchange does to a group of boys who have just discovered that remorse can be produced on demand and that adults will pay for it. The confusion is theirs as much as anyone's: they can no longer tell which of their own apologies they mean.

The version shown at Venice in 1997 ran a hundred and twenty-five minutes, and its makers left the festival announcing they would cut it. What remains is a hundred and one minutes in which Naples is held against its own antiquity: a narrator moving among Nero, his mother Agrippina, the Sibyl of Cumae and the martyr Artema, while a modern family, pushed out to the countryside by the earthquakes of the seventies, loses the closeness that had held it together. Gaudino was making his first feature and saw no reason to keep the two eras in separate rooms. The experiment is in the joinery, in whether a ruined imperial coast and a poor household two thousand years later can share one film without either being reduced to a figure for the other.

Two men in pain go looking for a cure and keep turning up versions of each other. Nilthamrong routes that search through imagination rather than incident, so across a hundred and three minutes the ordinary supports, who these men are and how their paths touch and what one passage owes the next, are deliberately slack. The Thai title is the English phrase spelled out in Thai letters, a borrowed name for the point at which a line stops being visible without ever stopping. Thailand, 2015. The business of the film is whether two separate lives can be shown to rhyme, and whether a rhyme like that is consolation or coincidence; nearly everything a drama usually supplies has been set aside to get there.

A mother is sterilising jars for the winter pickling while, in the next room, her daughter practises karaoke for an audience of one small brother. Out in the shed a young man does work nobody will be declaring, his acting plans shelved. By evening the household will be at the opening of the new canning factory where the father works, the same preserving scaled up to industry. Achard allows himself one weekend, eighty-six minutes and a single house, then lets the arrival of a woman nobody was expecting do the rest. Nothing is announced as important. The pressure comes from proximity: how few rooms these people have, and how thoroughly each of them already knows what the others have given up on.

None of these images were shot by the director; they were filmed and broadcast by the people inside them. They are Chinese live-streamers with small followings, several of them kept from easy face-to-face life by disability, poverty, or who they are. Zhu Shengze's work is the cutting: two hours of other people's uploads arranged until a pattern shows through, and the pattern is how much of a life a person will hand to strangers in exchange for being watched. IFFR audiences voted it their prize, an unusual result for a collage made of material its maker never staged. Companionship is the word it keeps testing. Whether the version conducted through a phone is a substitute for the other kind or simply another kind is left standing as a live question.

On the islands off Iran's southern coast, a living is made by moving goods past the people paid to stop them. Lavafipour's first feature stays with the families who do it rather than with the traffic, which is only work: the waiting, the debts, what a household does on a day when a boat is late. The style is plain to the point of severity, no invented drama laid over the daily one, and at eighty-nine minutes it does not outstay what it has seen. What is at risk is small and total at once. A crossing that goes badly out there produces no headline anywhere; it removes one of the few people a house is built around, and the next boat goes anyway, because nobody has offered these islands an alternative.

She leaves Bangkok for an isolated farm, to meet the family of the man she is going to marry. Everything after that is a question of tempo. A hundred and five minutes, a household that has known one another for decades, one guest with no history in the place: what the film owes itself is hospitality, silence, the long middle of an afternoon. Kongsakul lets it be filed as romance, though the courtship is settled before the first scene and the real matter is whether a person can be taken into somebody else's ground and kept there. The isolation is not atmosphere. It is the practical condition of the story, since there are no neighbours to dilute the encounter and nowhere to go when the day gets long.

The job is bending paperclips: not manufacturing them, bending them, a post a factory apparently needs filled. Kogure fills it. Ikeda builds ninety-nine minutes on a stoical loser whose routine fits in one sentence, then puts a butterfly in his flat and lets her become his wife, which is where the deadpan starts doing real work. The comedy is in the flatness: a world pared back to the fewest possible objects and played entirely straight, so that an impossible marriage arrives with the same weight as a shift change. Japan, 2014, and the wife turns out stranger than the minimal life she has moved into. Whether Kogure has been rewarded or further reduced by any of it stays open, which is how a joke this dry manages to be sad.

The family is a real one, and the father's drinking is theirs, not a screenwriter's device. Zhang Yuan took his material from a Beijing household whose damage was already in place, the mother holding the arrangement together and the sons of the title inside it. Ninety-five minutes leaves no room for a slow accumulation of causes, so the film opens in the middle of the pattern, on a day like the ones before it. What it does is closer to attention than to storytelling. The drinking is not explained and the marriage is not adjudicated; the young men are given the job of being present in a place they did not build and cannot repair. China in 1996, and the distance between a real family and a story about one is exactly what the film declines to close.

Since 2014 the villages of Cameroon's Far North Region have been struck often enough that the threat is no longer an event but a condition of the day. Cyrielle Raingou films from inside that condition. Woven-in is the operative idea: a danger absorbed into routine stops generating scenes and starts generating habits, and habits are what seventy-six minutes of documentary can actually hold. The obvious film would go where the violence is. This one stays in the hours between, where the arithmetic of an ordinary morning has quietly been rewritten and nobody remarks on it. What the title names is an organisation. What the film records is the shape a population takes once the danger has stopped being news.

What they steal is an electric guitar, out of the bar at an ice rink, during the May Day holiday of 1979. Alma Ata, three boys loose on their spring break, sixty-five minutes: Karakulov needs no more, because only one part of this machine has to move. Valera's father finds the guitar and hands his son to the police. Everything the film has to say about that decision is in what the police then do, and in how fast the other two understand that nobody official is coming to their side of it. Made in Kazakhstan in 1997 and looking back eighteen years at a Soviet spring, it is less curious about what teenagers get up to than about what a father believes he is doing when he picks the state over his own son.

Three brothers come together at the family's summer house out in the country. Their father is missing, so the arrangement they have to work out among themselves has nothing at the top of it. Kazama takes a hundred and fourteen minutes over this, unhurried for a premise that could be dispatched in seventy, and the unhurriedness is the method: grievances between brothers do not surface on schedule. Then a cousin arrives, a woman who is family without being party to any of it, and the house reorganises around her. Japan, 1995, and the tensions were boiling before anyone arrived. What Kazama is good at is the specific ugliness available to siblings who know one another's weak points exactly and have the rest of the season in which to use them.

Three hours and nine minutes about a woman with no crisis in her life. Matsushita Hikari is in her early thirties, employed, untroubled, surrounded by people whose difficulties have at least given them someone to hold onto; she has no such ballast, and the lack of it begins to worry her. The length is not decoration. A life without an emergency has to be filmed close to its real duration or it registers as nothing at all, and the ordinary business of days is what Tanaka uses to make her unease legible. On a trip into the mountains of Hokkaido she meets Masato, a Deaf landscape photographer. From there the film concerns itself with how one person's way of attending to the world can rearrange another's.

An old woman who herds goats is told that money is finally coming for what her father did in the war, and the offer is a swindle. That is the whole of the incident. Jacobs builds the remaining sixty-five minutes out of return instead: the same views, the same tasks, come back to and altered, which is what he gives in place of a plot. Repetition is a hard structure to sustain and an honest one for a life measured in chores. Afrikaans, South Africa, and the debt at the centre is real even if the payment is not, a service performed decades ago in somebody else's war and left unsettled long enough to become useful to a con man. Endurance is not being praised here. It is shown as what stays available to a person once compensation has stopped being a possibility.
